For the global shipping industry the inter-war years proved to be among the most challenging of the twentieth century. Significant shifts occurred in the commodity make-up of international trade. For example, the growth of oil shipments required more tanker vessels. Technological developments affected construction methods and ship propulsion systems. By 1939 about a quarter of the world fleet was powered by diesel engines. The overriding feature of the period, however, was that the supply of shipping services greatly exceeded the demand. World trade grew far more slowly than in either the pre-1914 or post-1945 periods, while more and more countries developed mercantile fleets on a significant scale for reasons of defence, prestige or as part of their natural economic development (Figures 1 and 2)These trends presented a significant challenge to the more established shipping nations, not just to the actual owners of the ships but also to their respective governments. By the 1930s most countries had decided on one of two paths. The fleets of the United States, Japan, France, Germany and Italy received significant government support via subsidies, construction loans and flag discrimination. The aim was to defend or develop particular services or particular types of shipping provision and there was little attempt to disguise the fact that non-commercial criteria were partially driving policy. Conversely in the Netherlands, Greece and the Scandinavian countries --all of whom did a considerable amount of carrying on behalf of other nations--national governments decided they had more to lose than gain from an international subsidy race. Owners therefore received little state help beyond small postal subsidies and some modestly favourable credit facilities to expedite new ship construction. In effect, ship owners were left to fend for themselves and find opportunities for expansion using their own entrepreneurial skills. (1)

Outcomes were mixed but the rationale behind each approach was fairly clear. However, the nation with the largest mercantile marine of all, namely Britain, presents a more complex and confusing picture. In the 1920s British governments were firmly in the non-subsidisers' camp. In the 1930s this was no longer the case as legislative packages involving subsidies and construction loans were enacted to benefit British owners. Yet these aid efforts seemed half-hearted. Provision was sporadic, small in scale (at least until 1939), and seemed to lack a strategic purpose. Help was given in ways that did little to enhance the competitive ability of the British mercantile marine or fulfil any other obvious criteria.The present article examines this paradox. Why did the country which in 1918 saw maritime supremacy as integral to its global status and a cornerstone of national economic development seem unable to formulate a coherent response to the challenges of the inter-war years? This question has attracted little attention previously in the historiography of British shipping. In the standard works state assistance is described, sometimes at length, and its impact evaluated. But there has been little analysis of the motive and intent of policy makers in terms of why they chose the course of action they did. (2)The next two sections establish the background to state policy. First there is a review of the economic difficulties confronting the British mercantile marine after 1918. In particular the respective contributions of exogenous and endogenous factors to relative decline are examined. Second there is a short evaluation of the British government's stance on shipping issues in the 1920s and the changes that occurred after the slump. The packages of shipping support provided in the 1930s are summarised and their limitations underlined in relation to the economic problems confronting the industry. The remainder of the article interprets state policy in the 1930s, drawing on hitherto neglected official records, and those of the main trade organisation, the Chamber of Shipping. It is suggested policy confusion was almost unavoidable in the circumstances of the time, given the attitude of the industry itself and the difficulty in reconciling shipping's particular problems with wider government objectives. The focus will be mostly on ocean-going shipping rather than coastal or short sea routes, as it was the former that absorbed most of Britain's tonnage at the time.

Economic backgroundThe importance of the mercantile marine to Britain was self-evident in 1914, when about 42 per cent of world steam and motor tonnage, amounting to some 18.9 million gross tons, sailed under the British flag (one gross ton = 100 [ft.sup.3] of hull space, which is approximately 2.7 [m.sup.3]). As well as making a major contribution to the balance of payments this fleet was also a potent expression, both practical and symbolic, of Britain's status as a major power. Heavy tonnage losses were sustained between 1914 and 1918, but they were largely made good by 1922. Fleet growth then continued but at a much slower pace than pre-war until 1931, when the British mercantile marine reached a peak of 20.2 million tons. Thereafter decline set in. Despite a slight upturn in the late 1930s the British fleet was over a million tons below its 1914 level in June 1938. (3)In part this faltering performance could be blamed on the sluggish growth of world seaborne trade, reflecting rising protectionism and global depression. However, there was no absolute decline in trade volumes and by 1938 the carriage of goods by sea was some 35 per cent higher than in 1913. (4) Many foreign fleets expanded to take advantage of this, and Britain's relative position declined in consequence (Table 1). Relative decline was not confined to any one part of the British fleet, although some branches suffered more than others. Tramp shipping (where vessels were chartered on a voyage or time basis, usually to carry dry bulk commodities like food and raw materials) experienced the biggest reverse. Having previously been the backbone of the mercantile marine, tramp tonnage dwindled by two-thirds between 1914 and 1938. In part this reflected a worldwide trend towards liner carriage between the wars. But British vessels commanded a diminishing share of the tramp business that remained as severe competition among the small firms that typified the sector drove the cost of goods carriage (hereafter referred to as 'freights') below pre-1914 levels. (5) The liner section (where vessels ran scheduled services, carrying mixed cargo and sometimes passengers) fared better. Business was expanding and price competition was less severe, reflecting in part the oligopolistic structure of the industry. The high fixed costs involved in providing regular services encouraged British and foreign lines to agree minimum terms of carriage via the so-called conference system. (6) Firms also tended to be large-scale. (7) As a result liner freights fell less than those for tramps after 1920 (Figure 3). Nevertheless British lines grew more slowly than most overseas rivals in the 1920s and thereafter the liner tonnage on the British register declined. (8) Some companies found themselves marginalised within conferences they had once dominated, particularly on Pacific and Indian Ocean routes. (9) It was a similar story in oil tankers. In quantum terms the growth of oil carriage was by far the most significant development in seaborne trade between the wars and the world tanker fleet grew from 1.5 million to 10.7 million gross tons between 1914 and 1938. But Britain's share of that total fell roughly from half to a quarter over the same period. (10)Some aspects of relative decline were beyond the control of ship owners, notably the contracting volume of trade passing through British ports between the wars. But, against this, intra-imperial commerce (which British ships dominated) was relatively buoyant in the 1930s. The greatest loss of market share came in trade between countries outside the empire, where competition was most severe. Between 1912 and 1936 Britain's share of world sea trade movements between non-empire ports fell by more than half (see F-F in Figure 4).Ship owners consistently refuted the notion that their own conduct was in any way responsible for these trends, blaming instead the growing tendency of foreign states to subsidise their fleets. (11) But, as Sturmey has shown, attributing the relative decline of British shipping principally to the machinations of overseas governments is problematic. The country that did most to support its mercantile marine was the United States, whose war expanded fleet had reached 14.2 million tons by 1922. But outside the protected lake and coastal trades this vast armada struggled to make its mark, due to high operating costs. By 1939 a mere 2.5 million tons was still engaged in international trade. (12) The main subsidisers in Europe, namely France, Germany and Italy, also struggled, especially in the 1930s, when British shipping held its ground fairly well against their competition. By contrast two of the biggest gainers at British expense, Greece and Norway, gave their shipping relatively little help. (13)Why else then, was British shipping in relative decline? Labour costs were higher than in most other countries excluding the United States. Pre-war British owners had been able to offset this by investing in the most up-to-date, efficient vessels. Strained financial circumstances in the inter-war period made it more difficult to renew fleets, and from the mid-1920s onwards the average age of ships on the British register began to increase. By 1938 only about a third were under ten years old. (14) But faster fleet modernisation would not have been a panacea. Indeed, the British line that built most new tonnage in the 1920s, Royal Mail, collapsed in the world slump under a weight of debt. (15) Undoubtedly for some types of basic bulk cargo carriage low-wage centres like Greece and Japan now held a decisive competitive edge, and nothing could be done to reverse this. (16)However, this does not mean that high-wage countries were doomed to fail between the wars. The experience of the Norwegian mercantile marine is particularly instructive in this regard. Between the wars the Norwegian fleet more than doubled in size, reaching 4.6 million tons by 1938, 46 per cent of which was under ten years of age. This gave Norway the most modern fleet in the world. Yet Norway was not a low-wage competitor. Success came from exploiting market niches using specialised vessels.
